title: Friend Circle Queries
directAnswer: Each query (a, b) makes a and b friends; friendship is transitive, forming circles. After each query, report the size of the largest circle so far. Use union-find with a size per component and union by size: when two distinct circles merge, the new size is the sum; keep a running max and append it after every query. Because person IDs can be up to 10⁹, back the disjoint set with hash maps, not arrays. O(q · α) ≈ O(q).

remember.pattern: Union-find with component sizes + running max
rules: Track a **size per root** and merge **smaller into larger** (union by size) to keep trees shallow.
Maintain a **running max** circle size; update it only when a union actually merges two *different* circles.
Person IDs are huge (up to 10⁹) → back parent/size with **hash maps**, lazily creating a singleton (size 1) on first sight.
A query joining two people **already in the same circle** changes nothing — `best` stays the same; still append it.
Append the current `best` after **every** query, including no-op unions.
whenToUse: Incremental **merging** of groups with a 'largest group so far' question
Dynamic connectivity: edges arrive online, queries interleave
Sparse / large id space where arrays won't fit → hash-map DSU
You only need group *sizes/connectivity*, not paths or distances
antiSignals: Edges are *removed* over time → union-find can't undo; use other structures (or offline + reverse)
You need shortest paths or weighted distances → Dijkstra/BFS, not DSU
A static graph asked once → a single BFS/DFS pass suffices
You must enumerate each group's members repeatedly → maintain explicit lists, not just sizes
remember.takeaway: Union-find is the canonical tool for online merging plus connectivity. Augmenting each root with a size turns 'how big is the largest group?' into an O(1) running maximum updated on each real merge — the standard pattern behind friend circles, islands that grow, and accounts-merge problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you model incremental friend-merging as union-find, augment it with per-component size, and maintain the largest size as a running max — using hash maps because IDs are large.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Recomputing component sizes by BFS after each query (O(q·n)), updating the max on no-op unions, forgetting union by size / path compression, or assuming small array-indexable IDs.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Note that the max only changes on a real merge, use union by size + path compression for the inverse-Ackermann bound, and explain why a hash-map DSU is required for a 10⁹ id space.

problemStatement:
You are given a list of `q` queries. Each query is a pair `(a, b)` declaring that persons `a` and `b` are now friends. Friendship is **transitive**: if `a`–`b` and `b`–`c` are friends, then `a`, `b`, `c` form one friend circle.

After processing each query, record the size of the **largest friend circle** that exists at that moment. Return the list of these maxima, one per query.
constraints: 1 ≤ a, b ≤ 10⁹ (person IDs are large and sparse)
a ≠ b within a query (or, if equal, the union is a harmless no-op)
Friendships are permanent and undirected (never removed)
Output has exactly q entries — the running max after each query
understanding: People are nodes; each query adds an undirected edge, and a friend circle is a connected component. The twist is that everything is online — edges arrive one at a time and after each you must answer 'biggest circle so far'. Re-scanning the whole graph per query is too slow at 10⁵ queries. Union-find merges circles in near-constant time and, by storing each circle's size on its root, lets you track the largest size as a running maximum: it can only grow, and only when a query actually fuses two previously-separate circles. The huge id space forces a hash-map-backed DSU rather than plain arrays.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I report the max after every query, or only at the end?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: After every query — the output is a list of q running maxima.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large are the person IDs?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 10⁹ and sparse, so I'll back the disjoint set with hash maps and create singletons lazily.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if both people are already in the same circle?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The union is a no-op; the largest size is unchanged, but I still append the current max for that query.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can friendships be removed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — they're permanent. Union-find only supports merging, which is exactly enough here.

examples.explanation: After (1,2): circle {1,2} size 2 → max 2. After (3,4): circles {1,2},{3,4} both size 2 → max 2. After (2,3): they merge into {1,2,3,4} size 4 → max 4.
Second (1,2) is a no-op (same circle), max stays 2. (5,6) forms another size-2 circle; max is still 2.
A growing chain: sizes 2, then 3, then 4. Large sparse IDs handled by hash-map DSU.

approaches.name: Explicit-Set Merge (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention the literal model first: keep each circle as an actual set, and on a query merge one set into the other, repointing every moved member. Simple, but each merge can touch many members.
hints: Model a circle as a real set of members, and keep a map from each person to the set they belong to.
On query (a, b): if they're in different sets, pour the members of one set into the other and update each moved member's pointer; track the new size and the global max.
Merging without choosing the smaller side can move many members repeatedly → O(n) per merge in the worst case. Correct, but it motivates union-find.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each merge copies the members of one circle into another and repoints them. Without always moving the smaller side, a single person can be moved up to n times across q queries, giving O(q · n) worst case. Lookups are O(1) via the person→set map. Correct and intuitive, but quadratic in adversarial inputs.
approaches.explanation:
The most direct model treats each friend circle as a concrete collection of people.

**The structure.** A hash map `circleOf` maps each person to the set object representing their circle. New people start in a fresh singleton set.

**Per query.** For `(a, b)`, fetch both sets. If they're the same object, it's a no-op. Otherwise merge: iterate over the members of one set, add each to the other, and update its `circleOf` pointer to the surviving set. The surviving set's size is the sum; update the global `best` and append it.

**Why it's correct.** Sets exactly represent connected components: merging two sets on an edge models transitive friendship precisely, and the size of the largest set is the answer.

**Why we don't ship it.** Pouring all members of one set into another costs time proportional to that set's size. If you don't consistently move the *smaller* set, a chain of merges can re-move the same elements over and over — O(q · n). Union-find replaces whole-set copying with a single pointer update, dropping each operation to near-O(1).
approaches.insight: Explicit-set merging makes the model obvious, and even reveals the key optimization: always move the smaller set (small-to-large) to bound the work. Union-find generalizes that intuition with union by size plus path compression, avoiding member copying entirely.

dryRun.intro: circleOf maps person → set. Merge moves members of one set into the other.

java.line: Set<Integer> sa = circleOf.computeIfAbsent(a, x -> new HashSet<>(Set.of(x)));
java.explanation: Lazily create a singleton circle the first time a person appears.

java.line: if (sa.size() < sb.size()) { Set<Integer> t = sa; sa = sb; sb = t; }
java.explanation: Move the smaller set into the larger (small-to-large) to limit member copying.
Only a real merge can grow the largest circle.

python.line:
if len(sa) < len(sb):
                sa, sb = sb, sa
python.explanation: Ensure we iterate the smaller set.
Repoint each moved member to the surviving circle.

approaches.name: Union-Find with Size (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended solution. Phrase it as 'hash-map disjoint set with union by size and path compression; track a running max that updates only on a real merge'.
hints: Instead of copying members, can each circle be a tree of parent pointers so a merge is one pointer update?
Union-find: find(x) returns the root (circle id) with path compression; union(a, b) links the smaller-size root under the larger and adds the sizes.
Keep size[root] for each circle and a running best. On a real merge, best = max(best, new size). Append best after each query. Back parent/size with hash maps for the 10⁹ id space.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each query does two finds and at most one union. With path compression and union by size, those are O(α(n)) amortized (inverse Ackermann ≤ 4 in practice). So all q queries cost O(q · α(n)) ≈ O(q). Hash-map operations are O(1) average. Space is O(n) for the parent and size maps over the distinct people seen.
approaches.explanation:
Union-find turns whole-set merging into a single pointer change, keeping circle sizes on the roots.

**The structure.** Two hash maps: `parent[x]` (the parent pointer; a root points to itself) and `size[r]` (members in the circle rooted at `r`). The first time a person is seen, `find` creates them as a singleton — `parent[x] = x`, `size[x] = 1`.

**find with path compression.** `find(x)` walks parent pointers to the root and compresses the path so future lookups are near-constant.

**union by size.** For query `(a, b)`, compute roots `ra, rb`. If equal, the two are already in one circle — a no-op. Otherwise attach the smaller-size root under the larger and add the sizes. Union by size keeps the trees shallow, which (with path compression) gives the inverse-Ackermann bound.

**The running max.** The largest circle can only change when two different circles merge, and the only candidate for a new maximum is the just-merged circle's size. So after a real union, `best = max(best, size[newRoot])`; on a no-op, `best` is unchanged. Append `best` after every query — including no-ops — to produce exactly `q` outputs.

**Why hash maps.** IDs reach 10⁹ and are sparse, so an array of that size is infeasible. Hash maps store only the people actually involved, with lazy singleton creation on first contact.
approaches.insight: Augmenting union-find's roots with a size is the lever that answers aggregate questions ('largest circle', 'is this group big enough?') in O(1) per merge. Combined with the observation that the global max only moves on a real merge, the whole problem collapses to one running maximum updated alongside the unions.

dryRun.intro: parent/size hash maps; singletons created lazily (size 1). best starts 0.

java.explanation: Lazily register a never-seen person as their own singleton root.
Re-point every node on the path directly to the root to flatten future finds.

java.line: if (size.get(ra) < size.get(rb)) { int t = ra; ra = rb; rb = t; }
java.explanation: Union by size: attach the smaller circle under the larger.
The only candidate for a new global max is the freshly merged circle.

python.line:
if x not in parent:
            parent[x] = x
            size[x] = 1
            return x
python.explanation: First sighting → singleton circle of size 1.

python.line:
while parent[x] != root:            # path compression
            parent[x], x = root, parent[x]
python.explanation: Flatten the path so subsequent finds are near-constant.
Hang the smaller root beneath the larger.
Update the running max only on a real merge.

pitfalls: Updating best on a no-op union (same root).
Skipping union by size and/or path compression — finds degrade toward O(n).
Using arrays for parent/size when IDs reach 10⁹.
Re-deriving the max by scanning all components each query — that's O(q·n).

commonMistakes: Recomputing component sizes with BFS/DFS after each query — O(q·n) and too slow.
Updating the running max on a query that joins two already-connected people.
Forgetting union by size / path compression, degrading find toward O(n).
Indexing arrays by person ID when IDs are up to 10⁹ — use hash maps.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Max updated on a no-op union
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If a and b are already in the same circle, nothing merges. Touching best (or re-adding size) here can overcount, and re-summing sizes corrupts the component size.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
parent[rb] = ra            # blindly unions even if ra == rb
size[ra] += size[rb]
best = max(best, size[ra])
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
if ra != rb:               # only on a real merge
    parent[rb] = ra
    size[ra] += size[rb]
    best = max(best, size[ra])

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Array DSU with huge IDs
commonMistakesDetailed.why: IDs reach 10⁹, so new int[10⁹] is infeasible (memory) — and even compressing requires a map. A hash-map DSU stores only the people actually seen.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int[] parent = new int[1_000_000_001];   // out of memory
commonMistakesDetailed.good: Map<Integer, Integer> parent = new HashMap<>();   // lazy, sparse

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Rescanning for the max
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Deriving the largest circle by iterating all components after each query is O(n) per query → O(q·n). Maintaining a running max updated on each real merge is O(1).
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: result.append(max(size[find(p)] for p in all_people))  # O(n) per query
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
best = max(best, size[ra])   # O(1) update on merge
result.append(best)

patternNote: Canonical Union-Find with Augmented Size. Recognize it on online merging plus an aggregate query ('largest group', 'still connected?'). Store size on roots, union by size with path compression, and keep a running max updated only on real merges. Use a hash-map-backed DSU whenever the id space is too large or sparse for arrays.
